description: Currency notes for the 2023 thesis 'Direito, Saneamento e Sustentabilidade'. Each entry checks one claim, citation, or figure against its current real-world status. This does not alter the original thesis text; it is a separate, dated annotation layer. 'page' refers to the PDF page number used throughout this package (see review-adjudications.json for the same numbering).

entries.topic: Constitutionality of Lei 14.026/2020 (Marco Legal do Saneamento)
entries.thesis_claim: Text reports that critics argued Lei 14.026/2020 unconstitutionally transferred sanitation competencies to the private sector via ordinary law rather than constitutional amendment, 'demandando a atuação do Supremo Tribunal Federal' (citing PONTES, 2021), framing the question as pending.
entries.current_status: The STF ruled on this on 2 December 2021, over a year and a half before the thesis was defended (14 August 2023). By 7 votes to 3, the Plenary rejected four ADIs (6492, 6356, 6583, 6882) challenging the law, upholding its constitutionality on the grounds that sanitation is a matter of local interest within municipal competence.

entries.thesis_claim: Text describes these two decrees (published 5 April 2023) as the current regulatory update to the Marco Legal do Saneamento, revising rules on economic-financial capacity of service providers and regionalized service provision.
entries.current_status: Both decrees were revoked in July 2023, before the thesis's 14 August 2023 defense, and replaced by Decretos 11.598/2023 and 11.599/2023. The regulatory content described is no longer the operative text; the successor decrees should be checked for what changed.

entries.topic: SNIS as the national sanitation data source
entries.thesis_claim: Table 2 (Distribuição de Água Por Município No Brasil) and other statistics throughout the thesis cite SNIS (2020) as the source for national sanitation coverage data.
entries.current_status: SNIS was discontinued in 2023. It has been replaced by SINISA (Sistema Nacional de Informações em Saneamento Básico), which began operating in 2024 under the Ministério das Cidades (not ANA). SINISA has since published 2023, 2024, and 2025 sector reports. Any figure sourced from SNIS (2020) has a more recent SINISA equivalent to check against.

entries.topic: Marco Legal universalization target (2033: 99% water, 90% sewage)
entries.thesis_claim: Cites the legal target of universal water supply (99%) and sewage collection/treatment (90%) by 31 December 2033, per Lei 14.026/2020, without reporting a progress figure against that target.
entries.current_status: Two distinct metrics exist and should not be conflated: (1) IBGE's Censo 2022 (household self-report) found 62.5% of Brazilians connected to a sewage network nationally, up from 52.8% (2010) and 44.4% (2000): the same national trend underlying the thesis's own 2000/2010 municipal tables, now with a third data point. Water supply network access nationally is 82.9%. (2) Separately, ANA/sector-press figures (a different, narrower operational metric, tracked against the 2033 statutory target) put coverage lower, around 84.2% water and 55.8% sewage as of the most recent reporting found, with multiple 2026 analyses describing the 2033 target as unlikely to be met at the current investment pace. Both point the same direction (meaningful progress, target still far off), but cite whichever one matches the claim being checked, they are not interchangeable.

entries.topic: Table 3: investment needed for universalization (R$ 893 billion)
entries.thesis_claim: Table 3 reports ABCON SINDCON/KPMG's estimate of over R$ 893 billion needed for universalization (R$ 164bi water, R$ 436bi sewage), dated to the source used at the time of writing (2022 edition).
entries.current_status: More recent ABCON SINDCON figures put the total investment need at approximately R$ 1 trillion, with R$ 205 billion already contracted through 2033 and a further R$ 72.4 billion expected to be auctioned in 2025 alone. The R$ 893 billion figure is from an earlier edition of the same annual panel and should be updated if this table is cited going forward.

entries.topic: Caçador population and sanitation-access tables (5-8)
entries.thesis_claim: Tables 5-8 present Caçador's water supply, sewage, and waste collection access using Censo 2000 (regional) and Censo 2010 (municipal) data.
entries.current_status: Censo 2022 recorded Caçador's population at 73,720 (+4.18% vs. 2010). IBGE's 2022 census also carries updated household-level sanitation-access results for the municipality (water supply, sewage type, waste collection) that postdate the 2000/2010 figures in these tables by 12-22 years. The population baseline is confirmed here; the sanitation-access percentages themselves were not re-extracted in this pass and should be pulled from IBGE Cidades' Caçador panorama page directly.

entries.topic: Videira population and sanitation-access tables (9-12)
entries.thesis_claim: Tables 9-12 present Videira's water supply, sewage, and waste collection access using Censo 2000 (regional) and Censo 2010 (municipal) data.
entries.current_status: Censo 2022 recorded Videira's population at 55,466. As with Caçador, the underlying sanitation-access percentages in these tables predate the 2022 census by 12-22 years and were not re-extracted in this pass.

entries.topic: Concórdia population and sanitation-access tables (13-16)
entries.thesis_claim: Tables 13-16 present Concórdia's water supply, sewage, and waste collection access using Censo 2000 (regional) and Censo 2010 (municipal) data.
entries.current_status: Censo 2022 recorded Concórdia's population at 81,625. More significantly: CASAN (the state utility likely underlying the thesis's 2010-era Concórdia tables) has since been replaced. Concórdia Saneamento, a private concessionaire, took over water and sewage service in the municipality with a pledged R$ 300 million investment. As of the 2025 reporting found, sewage collection and treatment coverage stands at 25% of the municipality, with a stated target of 90% and treated-water losses at 53%. This is a live illustration of exactly the concession-driven-universalization dynamic the thesis's own abstract raises as a hypothesis, now playing out in one of its own three case-study cities.

entries.topic: Sault Ste. Marie population (cited as 73,368, 2016 census)
entries.current_status: 2021 Census of Canada recorded Sault Ste. Marie (city) at 72,051, a decline of about 1.8% from the 2016 figure cited. Canada's next census cycle is 2026, so an even newer figure will supersede this again once results are released (typically ~1 year after collection).

entries.topic: Thunder Bay population (cited as 107,909, 2016 census)
entries.current_status: 2021 Census of Canada recorded Thunder Bay (city) at 108,843, up about 0.9% from the cited 2016 figure. Minor drift, but the cited figure is one census cycle behind.

entries.topic: North Bay population (cited as 51,553, 2016 census)
entries.current_status: 2021 Census of Canada recorded North Bay (city) at 52,662, up about 2.2% from the cited 2016 figure.

entries.topic: Chatham-Kent population (cited as ~101,000, sourced to a 2012 encyclopedia entry)
entries.current_status: 2021 Census of Canada recorded Chatham-Kent (municipality) at 103,988. Close to the cited figure, but the source (a 2012 general encyclopedia entry, not a census) predates the 2016 and 2021 census cycles the thesis otherwise relies on for other cities, an inconsistency worth flagging on its own.

entries.topic: Woodstock population (cited as ~40,000, sourced to City of Woodstock, 2023)
entries.current_status: 2021 Census of Canada recorded Woodstock (city) at 46,705, about 17% higher than the thesis's 'cerca de 40.000' figure. This is the largest gap found in the six-city population set and is worth a closer look at what the 2023 city source was actually reporting (a projection, or an older municipal-boundary figure, might explain the difference).

entries.topic: Kenora population (cited as ~15,000, sourced to City of Kenora, 2020)
entries.current_status: 2021 Census of Canada recorded Kenora (city) at 14,967, essentially identical to the cited figure. No update needed.

entries.topic: Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks (MECP), Ontario
entries.thesis_claim: Table 4/glossary and figure sources cite the Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks by that name, dated 2019-2021 sources.
entries.current_status: As of September 2026, the ministry continues to operate under this same name (current minister: Todd McCarthy). No renaming found.

entries.topic: Ontario Clean Water Agency (OCWA)
entries.thesis_claim: Describes OCWA, created in the 1970s, as responsible for water/wastewater treatment and network maintenance in over 600 Ontario communities.
entries.current_status: OCWA remains an active Crown agency in 2025-2026, now reporting operation of over 1,000 water and wastewater facilities with a 98.84% agency-wide compliance score in its most recent inspection period. Still operating under the same name and mandate.

entries.topic: Santa Catarina state-level water and sewage coverage
entries.thesis_claim: The comparative framing treats Santa Catarina as the Brazilian reference point against Ontario, citing IBGE (2021) for state-level demographic context, without a state-level sanitation coverage figure.
entries.current_status: Censo 2022 puts Santa Catarina's water supply access at 89.59%, above the national average. Sewage network access is well below it: sector reporting puts the state at roughly 34% connected to a sewage collection network, with about 46% of residents lacking sewage network access altogether. Two sources phrase this slightly differently (network-only vs. broader 'adequate sewage' framing), so the exact percentage should be re-confirmed against IBGE Cidades' own Santa Catarina panel before being cited precisely. Marked 'still_current' because this is new information filling a gap, not a correction of an existing thesis figure.

entries.topic: Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and Clean Water Act, 2006 (Ontario)
entries.thesis_claim: Cites both statutes as the current legal framework for drinking water safety and source-water protection in Ontario, per 2002 and 2006 sources.
entries.current_status: Both statutes remain in force but are actively being amended as of late 2025/2026. The Building a More Competitive Economy Act, 2025 (Bill 56, passed 4 November 2025) already amended the Clean Water Act, 2006. A further bill, the Building Homes and Improving Transportation Infrastructure Act, 2026, proposes amendments to the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and a new Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025, including changes to Municipal Residential Drinking Water Systems regulation (O. Reg. 205/18), stated aims being reduced duplication and faster approvals for new wells/intakes. Some of this was still under public consultation at last check, so the final text may differ from the proposal.

entries.topic: City of North Bay By-law 2014-054 (septic system regulation)
entries.thesis_claim: Cites By-law 2014-054 as requiring regular pump-outs for septic systems near Trout Lake, the city's drinking water source.
entries.current_status: The by-law (City records it as '2014-54') is still in force: it requires septic tanks on properties along Trout Lake or watercourses draining into it to be pumped out at least every 3 years (permanent residences) or 5 years (seasonal). No repeal or amendment found.

entries.topic: Global SDG 6 progress framing
entries.thesis_claim: Frames the entire comparison around SDG 6 and SDG 11 without citing a specific global progress figure to benchmark against.
entries.current_status: The UN's 2026 SDG 6 Synthesis Report on Water and Sanitation (the system's input to this year's High-Level Political Forum, which reviewed SDG 6 and SDG 11 together) reports real gains between 2015-2024 (961 million people gained safely managed drinking water; 1.2 billion gained safely managed sanitation) but a 2030 target still far off: 2.2 billion people still lacked safely managed drinking water and 3.4 billion lacked safely managed sanitation in 2024. The report states a 6-fold increase in the current pace of progress is needed on water and 5-fold on sanitation to hit 2030 targets. Useful as an updated global anchor if the thesis's SDG framing is cited or extended.

entries.topic: Instituto Água e Saneamento / Trata Brasil municipal rankings
entries.thesis_claim: Cites Instituto Água e Saneamento (2021) as a source for municipal-level sanitation data used in the Caçador/Videira/Concórdia tables.
entries.current_status: Checked whether a newer edition of the annual 'Ranking do Saneamento' (published through 2026) could refresh these tables directly: it cannot. The ranking only covers Brazil's 100 most populous municipalities; Caçador, Videira, and Concórdia (all under 82,000 people) fall below that threshold and are not covered by it. A refresh for these three cities has to come from IBGE Cidades or the municipalities' own utilities/concessionaires directly, as found for Concórdia above, not from this ranking.

not_yet_checked.topic: Lei nº 14.675/2009 (Código Estadual do Meio Ambiente de Santa Catarina)
not_yet_checked.reason: Same result as the Lei 17.717/2019 check: Legal Data Hunter's Brazil coverage has no Santa Catarina state legislative source, so it cannot resolve or search this law either. Needs the ALESC portal directly. A coverage-gap report was filed with Legal Data Hunter on 2026-09-17 (report_id fd50ee7d-72b0-42c1-8d25-7022d5a1d084) requesting Santa Catarina state legislation (ALESC) and TJSC case law be added as sources.

not_yet_checked.topic: Lei nº 17.717/2019 (Política Estadual de Saneamento Básico de Santa Catarina)
not_yet_checked.reason: Tried three independent paths: (1) web search, no match under this number on ALESC's indexed pages; (2) Legal Data Hunter's resolve_reference (230+ jurisdiction legal database), returned resolved: false; (3) Legal Data Hunter's full-text search, returned only irrelevant federal-level and municipal-gazette noise, no Santa Catarina state legislation at all. Root cause found: Legal Data Hunter's Brazil coverage (checked via discover_sources) has no Santa Catarina state legislative source and no TJSC case law source, only federal legislation (BR/Planalto, from 2022), federal case law, municipal gazettes, and a handful of other state courts (Paraná, Bahia, Amazonas, Acre). This is a genuine database coverage gap, not evidence the law doesn't exist or is miscited. The only remaining path is ALESC's own portal search (leis.alesc.sc.gov.br) directly, queried by a human or a tool that can drive its search form, not a general search engine or a multi-jurisdiction legal database. A coverage-gap report was filed with Legal Data Hunter on 2026-09-17 (report_id fd50ee7d-72b0-42c1-8d25-7022d5a1d084) requesting Santa Catarina state legislation (ALESC) and TJSC case law be added as sources.
